keyTerms.definition: The ability of carbon to form four covalent bonds with other atoms.

questions.question: What two structural features of carbon allow it to form a large variety of compounds?
Define a saturated carbon compound and give an example.
questions.expectedAnswer: A compound with only single C–C bonds; e.g., ethane (C2H6).

questions.question: How does an unsaturated compound differ in bonding, and name two types of unsaturated hydrocarbons.
questions.expectedAnswer: It contains double or triple C–C bonds; alkenes (double bonds) and alkynes (triple bonds).

questions.question: Which historical experiment disproved the 'vital force' theory, and what was synthesized?
questions.expectedAnswer: Friedrich Wöhler in 1828 synthesized urea from ammonium cyanate.

questions.question: List two typical physical properties of carbon compounds and explain why they occur.
questions.expectedAnswer: Low melting/boiling points and poor electrical conductivity because intermolecular forces are weak and the molecules are non‑ionic.

activities.description: In pairs, one student acts as Friedrich Wöhler and the other as a skeptical chemist of the era. They reenact the preparation of urea from ammonium cyanate and discuss its impact on the belief in vital force.

realWorldApplications.title: Urea Production in Agriculture
realWorldApplications.explanation: Urea, first synthesized by Wöhler, is now manufactured on an industrial scale and used as a nitrogen fertilizer for crops.
realWorldApplications.question: Why is the laboratory synthesis of urea historically important for modern agriculture?
realWorldApplications.expectedAnswer: It showed that an organic compound could be made artificially, leading to large‑scale production of urea, which supplies essential nitrogen to plants.

realWorldApplications.title: Choosing Materials Based on Electrical Conductivity
realWorldApplications.explanation: Because carbon compounds are poor conductors, they are used as insulating materials in electrical applications.
realWorldApplications.question: How do the non‑conductive properties of carbon compounds influence their use in everyday items?
realWorldApplications.expectedAnswer: Their inability to conduct electricity makes them suitable for insulating components such as plastic casings and non‑metallic wiring sheaths.

coreNotes.heading: Carbon’s Tetravalency and Catenation
coreNotes.summary: Carbon can form four covalent bonds and link to other carbon atoms, creating countless compounds.
coreNotes.content:
Carbon has an atomic number of 6 and four valence electrons, giving it a tetravalent nature. Because each carbon can bond to up to four other atoms, it can also bond to other carbon atoms. This ability, called catenation, allows the formation of long chains, branched structures, and rings. The combination of tetravalency and catenation is the reason for the very large number of carbon‑containing compounds.

• Tetravalent: forms four covalent bonds

• Catenation: carbon‑carbon bonding creates chains, branches, cycles

coreNotes.heading: Classification of Hydrocarbons
coreNotes.summary: Hydrocarbons are grouped as alkanes, alkenes, or alkynes based on the type of carbon‑carbon bonds they contain.
coreNotes.content:
All compounds that contain only carbon and hydrogen are called hydrocarbons. When every carbon‑carbon bond is a single bond, the hydrocarbon is saturated and is named an alkane. If one or more carbon‑carbon double bonds are present, the compound is unsaturated and called an alkene. When one or more carbon‑carbon triple bonds occur, the compound is an alkyne. These names reflect the bond type present in the molecule.

• Alkane – only single C–C bonds (saturated)

• Alkene – at least one C=C double bond (unsaturated)

• Alkyne – at least one C≡C triple bond (unsaturated)

coreNotes.heading: Saturated vs. Unsaturated Carbon Compounds
coreNotes.summary: Saturated compounds contain only single bonds; unsaturated compounds contain double or triple bonds.
coreNotes.content:
A saturated carbon compound has the maximum number of hydrogen atoms attached to each carbon because all carbon‑carbon connections are single bonds. Unsaturated compounds have fewer hydrogen atoms because double or triple bonds replace some C–H bonds. For example, ethane (C₂H₆) is saturated, while ethene (C₂H₄) is unsaturated due to a C=C double bond.

• Saturated → all single C–C bonds

• Unsaturated → one or more C=C or C≡C bonds

coreNotes.heading: Historical Milestone – Wöhler’s Synthesis of Urea
coreNotes.summary: Wöhler’s 1828 preparation of urea from ammonium cyanate disproved the vital‑force theory of organic synthesis.
coreNotes.content: It was once believed that organic compounds could only be produced by living organisms because a ‘vital force’ was required. In 1828, Friedrich Wöhler synthesized urea, an organic compound, from the inorganic ammonium cyanate. This experiment showed that organic molecules can be created in the laboratory without any vital force, marking the birth of modern organic chemistry.

coreNotes.heading: Physical Properties of Carbon Compounds
coreNotes.summary: Carbon compounds generally have low melting/boiling points and do not conduct electricity.
coreNotes.content:
Data on carbon compounds show they melt and boil at lower temperatures than ionic substances, indicating weak intermolecular forces. They are also poor conductors of electricity, which means their bonding does not produce ions. These properties arise because the molecules are held together mainly by weak van der Waals forces rather than strong ionic bonds.

• Low melting & boiling points

• Non‑conductive (no ions)

• Weak intermolecular attractions

coreNotes.heading: Structural Variety – Chains, Branches, and Rings
coreNotes.summary: Carbon atoms can arrange into straight chains, branched chains, or cyclic (ring) structures, each being saturated or unsaturated.
coreNotes.content:
Because of catenation, carbon atoms can link in several ways:

• Straight (linear) chains – e.g., methane, ethane

• Branched chains – carbon atoms form side‑branches off the main chain

• Cyclic structures – carbon atoms close to form a ring, such as benzene (C₆H₆)
Each of these frameworks may be saturated (only single bonds) or unsaturated (containing double or triple bonds).
